spec.title: Zap branding and task model policy

status.comment: Owner additions of 2026-09-15: Zap is the whole system, Zap Quick Lens is the user-facing client, Zap Wayfinder is its central component, and users configure task-to-model tiers and reasoning effort. This contract extends the active implementation plan.

p.branding: Zap names the complete system. Zap Quick Lens is the external name of the current practical browser/Electron client; quicklens remains its internal code identifier. Zap Wayfinder names the central shared coordination/server component. Other Lens implementations are components of Zap rather than competing umbrella products. Existing package group org.vibevm.zap, module paths, CLI compatibility and protocol identifiers do not require mechanical renaming merely to change display branding. User-facing headers, titles, help and documentation use the agreed external names.

p.model-routing: A versioned Zap model policy maps explicitly identified task classes and purposes to one of four model tiers plus an independent reasoning-effort request. Tiers are ultra, big, medium and small. Initial Codex bindings are ultra to gpt-6-astra, big to gpt-5.6-sol, medium to gpt-5.6-terra and small to gpt-5.6-luna. Bindings are configurable provider/model profiles; common planning and execution code does not infer tier, price or capability from a model name. Existing ZAP work type, role assessment and semantic routing remain distinct from these concrete execution preferences.

p.task-rules: Rules select tasks by declared class/purpose and applicable execution scope rather than guessing from a display title. Implementation work and LLM actors invoked for product testing are separate purposes. Coding profiles are chosen according to complexity and budget; actual test actors default to a low-cost suitable profile. The selected rule, policy identity/revision, tier and concrete profile are retained with the execution selection. Ambiguous rules, missing bindings or disallowed profiles produce explicit resolution results, not a silent premium fallback.

p.effort-capabilities: Effort support is described for the concrete product, version, model, execution mode and invocation scope, distinguishing coordinator, native child and any relevant fresh/forked invocation: configurable with supported values, inherited from the parent, unsupported or unknown. Requested effort, resolved configuration and actual host observation are separate. An inherited effort records its parent/source and available effective value without pretending a child flag changed it; inheritance of effort does not imply inheritance of the model. A model match with an unreported effort does not confirm the full selection. Explicit unsupported values or unknown capabilities are not silently discarded. Default/inherit choices remain explicit.

p.capability-evidence: Capability profiles and observed model/effort are trusted adapter evidence, not user-supplied authority. Provider-wide permanent assumptions are avoided. Current Claude Code documentation describes inherited effort by default and an optional subagent effort override; extended-thinking inheritance is a separate setting. This does not establish support in every installed version or invocation mode. A native-inherited profile remains valid where that mode is actually constrained. Codex is the only initial live test target; other-provider capability cases can be exercised as labelled fixtures.

p.policy-lifecycle: Users can inspect and change authorized task rules and tier bindings through Zap Wayfinder and the shared client contracts. Changes use an expected policy revision and retain history. New policy revisions apply to future selections/attempts; running sessions retain their recorded selection and are not restarted merely because preferences changed. A per-task override is explicit and recorded. Public policy data contains model/profile references and capability information, never provider credentials.

p.policy-interface: Zap Quick Lens presents task class, model tier and effort as separate controls, showing the concrete resolved model. In inherited or unsupported modes, the effort control explains its actual source or unavailability instead of offering an ineffective selector. Agent/output views distinguish requested/resolved values from later host-observed values. The same data and behavior are available to other Zap clients through shared server services; the UI does not implement a separate resolver.

p.verification: Focused deterministic tests cover four configurable tiers, task-rule selection, ambiguity/missing capability refusal, explicit effort, inherited effort without model inheritance, unavailable effort and preservation of an existing running selection. Policy persistence and UI integration are exercised through the shared application service. These are ordinary unit/integration tests, not a need to invoke large LLMs. The existing bounded-verification and account-independent checkpoint discipline remains in force.
